questions.questionText: `check_setup.py` prints your account and caller ARN, but then the model call fails for both models. Where is the problem most likely?
questions.explanation:
STS worked, so the identity is good. The remaining causes are missing Bedrock permissions, the wrong Region, or the Anthropic first-time use form not yet submitted.

(A) Printing the account and ARN means the STS "who am I?" call worked, so your credentials are fine.

(C) An old Python only prints a warning near the top of the output. It does not make the model call fail by itself.

options.optionText: Your AWS credentials, because they are not working
Permissions, the Region or model access, because only the model call failed
Your Python version, because it is older than 3.10

questions.questionText: Why do the model IDs in this course start with `global.`?
questions.explanation:
That is why it works from any supported source Region, including India, and why a bare model ID can fail with "on-demand throughput isn't supported".

(A) You still pay per token. The prefix has nothing to do with price.

(B) It does the opposite. A `global.` profile lets Bedrock route the request to whichever Region can serve it.

options.optionText: It makes the model free to call
It tells Bedrock to keep the request inside one Region
It is a cross-Region inference profile that routes each call to a Region with capacity

questions.questionText: In Step 4 you ask for the time in Bangalore and in New York. How many times does the model request `current_time`?
questions.explanation:
That is the agent loop with real tools: two requests, two results, then the final answer.

(A) The tool takes one timezone per call, so one request cannot cover both cities.

(B) A model has no clock. It only knows the time from a tool, which is why the tool exists.

options.optionText: Once, with both cities in a single argument
Never, because the model already knows the time
Twice, once per timezone, and then it answers from the two results

questions.questionText: Why does Step 5 give the agent the prebuilt `calculator` tool?
questions.explanation:
The GST question has an exact answer, 15,299.82. The calculator computes it rather than the model guessing.

(B) One tool, or none, is fine. Step 3 builds an agent with no tools at all.

(C) That overstates it. The page says LLMs are surprisingly unreliable at arithmetic, which is why exact sums go to a tool.

options.optionText: So the sum is computed exactly instead of "in its head", where LLMs are unreliable
An agent must have at least two tools to work
The model cannot do any maths, so every number needs a tool

questions.questionText: What does the system prompt in Step 6 do?
questions.explanation:
It works like the day-one briefing for a new employee. It applies to every customer request that follows.

(A) The user's question is still sent. The system prompt is extra instruction that sits alongside it.

(C) Tools are passed with `tools=[...]`. The system prompt is only text that shapes behaviour.

options.optionText: It replaces the user's question on every turn
It sets the agent's role, tone and rules for every turn of the conversation
It gives the agent a new tool to call
